p: The state authorizing bill is only for 600 intersections. The 1,350 was the original negotiation point in the 2025–
[interposing] Oh, okay.

negotiations for the reauthorization. That reflected, I think, a 10 percent of all intersections which is

where that number came from. But we’re only authorized up to 600 intersections.

Okay. So, given that it’s 600 would that concurrently– in terms of the ratio of the amount of revenue generated, do you foresee that being the same sort of ratio of the revenue that’s being generated in proportion?

Chair, just to highlight what the Commissioner said earlier. If we generated zero revenue, that’ll be a successful program. This is not a revenue-based program, and you know, we’re just trying to change drive behavior.
I’m sorry, can you repeat that?

Just to highlight what the Commissioner said earlier, if we generated zero dollars in revenue, that will be a successful program. We’re never looking at it as a revenue-based program. It’s more about changing driver behavior.

Agree, but you know, I think when we’re looking for, you know, ways to generate– it’s just– I guess I’m just not asking

about the intent, but it’s more about do you foresee that if there’s more redlight cameras there would be in theory more revenue.

And to speak at a high level, I think one of the things that we see is in the initial period where installation happens, there is a spike, right? People are unfamiliar. But what we also see is that driver behavior improves. So, I don’t think we can say for the status quo number for what you see in your metrics there, that would be indicative of what we would see in a scaler [sic] program.

Okay. I mean, yes, just for the record, I agree. We want to change driver behavior. That’s the ultimate goal, but I’m just trying to get a sense since it’s a budget hearing, right, of where you think the numbers will land. Okay. Does DOT expect– oh, what neighborhoods have seen the highest increase from camera revenue?
We don’t have that information with us today.

Okay. Were cameras moved with the aim of increasing– hold on. What is the error rate– sorry. What is the error rate for

red light camera violations? Do you have that information?
Sorry, what do you mean by that exactly?
If there are, for example– if there’s a car that mistakenly got this or there’s a license plate– I’m just trying to figure out if there are any errors and what that percentage would be and accuracy?

Okay. We have a very robust review process where we have a city employee reviewing each and every violation before it’s issued. We have an extremely high rate. Like, we don’t receive them back in error. We can get you the exact percentages.
Okay. And what is the process actually for the violation review?

So, we have DOT employees in our Traffic Operations Division who have been carefully trained for all the different camera type violations to examine each and every video, obviously looking at it carefully, confirming if it’s red light, confirming that in fact the signal has changed, where the vehicle is in the

intersection. There’s an SOP and a very detailed protocol of how that evaluation is made, and then that person certifies that it is a valid violation before it is issued.
Okay. And so, I think you’re sort of answering my question, but for the record, have any cameras been removed because of technical problems or excessive false tickets?

We would never get to the point of issuing a false ticket. If there’s any technical problem with the camera, we would work with the vendor to bring that back online, but if there were any issue we would not even consider those violations.
Okay, perfect. And how often are yellow light timings reviewed and adjusted?
How often is it calibrated or checked? Is that the question?
Yes.
I need to confirm that unless any of my colleagues have that.
Because I know that some traffic lights have longer yellow light timings versus others. So, just wanted to see.
We’ll have to get back to you on that.
Okay. And have you done any studies about whether extending the yellow light duration reduces violations or reduces people–

[interposing] So, the yellow phase is set as basically a ratio of the speed limit. So, whatever speed we expect drivers to be going or that they should be going or staying under, that’s what the timing’s based on. And so it shouldn't really be a variable thing in terms of the results if that makes sense.
Okay. What engineering alternatives were considered besides enforcement cameras? I know that you explained some of them.

Yeah, it’s not– I don’t think it’s really– we don’t approach it as an either/or. I think it’s really all of the above, and I just really want to stress how effective automated enforcement has been and how we see it, but also that 96 percent of drivers don’t get more than two

violations. So, we really– again, from our vantage point, it is a safety tool, and you know, and it’s a very effective one. So, we really appreciate the Council’s partnership also since we have to go back to the state every few years to get these programs reauthorized.

Right. Okay. So, moving onto the process to obtain traffic calming measures, because I know that this is the case in my neighborhood as well, especially in the parts of southeast Queens in my district where either around schools or, you know, in certain intersections there are very long sort of like streets between the avenues, because it’s a very long distance and people speed by. And so in the situation where community members would like four-way stop signs, it seems like the process itself to want to have other traffic calming measures aside from the cameras, right, whether it’s a speed bump or four-way stop signs, it seems like a very arduous process to go through that many community members are not understanding, especially if they have the signatures from the streets and their neighbors to want to get something like this done. And I know that usually DOT comes

out and does a study and observes, but I think oftentimes the frustration is it’s not during the times where kids get let out or where there’s a lot of parents in one area, right, especially around the schools. And so just wondering if you could walk us through the process to obtaining other traffic calming measures and what factors does DOT consider in that?

Sure. I can start. You know, I think– we certainly don’t want the processes to feel arduous. I think, you know, we’ve tried to create good pages on our website that explain these, but always open to feedback about how we can make it easier for the community to let us know, you know, what issues they’re facing. The other point I would make is just that, you know, again, we do try to approach these things holistically. So, it’s helpful for us to hear from the community what’s the issue, what’s the challenge, and then we can work with them to figure out what the right solutions might be. It may be a speed hump. It may be a stop sign. It may be a traffic signal. It could be something else. But if they want to request like a

specific tool, then we do have, you know, processes for each of those. You can speak a little more.

Right. And the processes all work together. Someone requests a stop sign, and we think it’s not appropriate for a stop sign. We don’t say, well, sorry, nothing we can do here. If we see speeding, then a speed hump might be appropriate or other traffic calming. We do try to take the concern and find the right treatment. And you know, we definitely hear about the times of day and things. You know, our signal engineers do go out and look at many times of day. It’s also helpful when we get feedback. You know, there’s a location where it turned that, you know– somewhere Saturdays there was a big little league thing that goes on, and so a weekday check which is usually the busiest time of the city wasn’t quite right, but because we heard about that traffic pattern, we could go out and look differently. So, the more information we get, the better we can be responsive to exactly what’s going on there.

Okay. And the new initiative that the Mayor had outlined which was the SPEED initiative, I mean, is this– something like

this, would that be included in terms of helping with the process of getting those things in place?
Chair, do you mean the state law, to stop super speeders, or–
[interposing] No, no, no. The thing that was in your testimony.
Oh, the SPEED–
[interposing] SPEED, yeah.
to speed up affordable housing and other sustainable development?

Yes. Because I know that you were saying– well, I mean in terms of the processes, and it says for example your portion was to hire eight positions. So, is that just for DOT alone? It’s not for the other agencies, right?
Correct, yeah.

Okay. And this is– I know it’s for– to help support critical housing, but it’s also transportation public infrastructure projects moving forward faster. So, I just wanted to clarify if something like this could also be included in that, or no?

Yeah. So, yes. This is giving us more resources to basically do the traffic studies, essentially, which is sometimes on the critical path for these developments, and you know, it’s one important step. So, by having the resources we need on that team, we’ll be able to process those reviews a lot faster.

Okay. And if this is sort of alluding to new developments, I would encourage that if this could be done overall, that’d be great, too. In terms of just the overall processes. So, I just wanted to make a note of that. In terms of vacancy reduction, Executive Plan includes baseline funding of $3 million starting in fiscal 27 from 49 headcount positions. So, what were these 49 positions that were eliminated and how will DOT be able to carry out the functions?

Sure. I can say to start, you know, that the vacancy reduction was done in tandem with the ending of the two-for-one hiring policy. So, while, you know, it’s a reduction in sort of theoretical headcount, it’s actually a lot more helpful for us to have real headcount that we can allocate, you know, based on the needs. So, in

the end, this is really a net positive for us. Igor could talk more about the specifics, but that’s how kind of we’re looking at it.

Thank you, Commissioner. So, we looked at all of our vacancies and looked at longstanding vacancies. There were a couple parts of the agency that just weren’t able to hire for a long time. So, to the Commissioner’s point, to allow us to enable hiring faster with the reduction of the two-for-one hiring freeze, we were going to take some vacancies down and hopefully that’ll help us speed up hiring for all of our other positions in need.
Okay. And is the entire Office of Sustainable Delivery being eliminated? If not, what positions remain and what will be the scope of the office?

No, we’re definitely keeping that function. I think we’ve rebranded it as Sustainable Delivery Unit, as you mentioned. Still a very important, you know, focus area for us to ensure delivery worker safety and safe behavior and we’re– well, yeah, we could talk more about, I guess, the specific headcount, but basically we’re focusing the

group more on the policy and regulatory approach needed to get safer outcomes in the delivery bike space versus, you know, an enforcement forward approach.

Great. And I know that you mentioned this earlier with the contractor that you re-bid for a lower cost, and so are there other savings measures like that were you’re looking at different consulting contracts or other areas? Because I know some of the agencies haven’t looked at actually some of their consulting contracts in years, and so just wondering if you guys have done a review of that.

Thank you for the question, Chair. So we’re constantly looking at all of our contracts, both professional services engineering contracts and seeing if there’s efficiencies that could be made. For contracts that are already in place, it’s a little bit hard because the terms are set. But every time we rebid we look at ways to do it faster and better. And to the question you asked earlier, there were three vendors that bid on the enforcement

contract, and Veer [sic] Mobility was the chosen vendor.
Great. And last question before I pass it off to the Chair. Is DOT looking to use technology training or deployment any differently to find efficiencies in its operations?

Absolutely, and this is, you know, an important priority for me honestly. I mean, I think it’s something that we do as a standard practice, but I really want to take a holistic look across the board at how we can improve our operations and efficiency, technology being one critical piece of that. And you know, we’re going to have folks really whose role is specifically focused on efficiency and organizational excellence.
Great. Thank you. And just quickly, we’ve been joined by Justin Sanchez and Christopher Marte. And Chair, go ahead.

Thank you, Chair Lee. This is a question for Commissioner Beaton. Deputy Commissioner Beaton, in April of last year you testified under oath to this committee that as it pertains to the cost of daylighting, 10,000 is a very round rule of thumb number for a single intersection.

You further emphasized this cost to Streets Block saying the cost of hardened daylighting infrastructure comes at about $10,000 per location which includes labor and regular maintenance. However, in that same hearing, your submitted testimony to the committee stated universal hardened daylighting would cost in the neighborhood of $3 billion. New York City has 40,000 intersections, Mr. Beaton, at a cost of $10,000 per intersection, it comes to $400 million. Is this just a simple case of bad math or a huge disagreement you have with yourself?

So, the $10,000 was per location. An intersection four corners, each corner can have two sides that are daylit. So, I think that that’s the discrepancy is it’s not per intersection, it’s per location.
I mean even if you were to multiply that by four, it will still be far less than the $3 billion in your testimony, is that correct?
Well,--
[interposing] Answer that question, is that correct?
To get a full number, you would multiply by eight. So, again, these are round numbers, but that’s how you get there.

Are you aware that the previous administration’s OMB estimates for Intro 1138 which called to daylight 1,000 intersections per year included several large additional costs, including $8.7 million for hardening barrier materials, $1.2 million for personnel services including fringe to hire staff, $5.5 million for annual personnel services, $780,000 for dry rails, and $420,000 for signage, $63,000 in year one, and $126 in year two for the purchasing of new vehicles, and we still only average to close to just $17,000 per intersection.

So, that is an average for one intersection. It doesn’t scale up equally, and with every number there’s always outliers. So, to the point Deputy Commissioner Beaton was making, you can just take one intersection and extrapolate that linearly.
This is an OMB estimate for Intro 1138, which is 1,000 intersection per year.

I think when you're picking a limited number of intersections, you can intentionally look for ones that are more straightforward and cost less. When you’re talking universally and doing it at every location in the city, you inherently have to do all the more complex ones, and so we– as Igor said, it doesn’t scale exactly the same way.
I think at the end of the day we’re eager to sit down and work through the details and if it’s a matter of figuring out what’s the most accurate cost, you know, we’re happy to be a partner in that.

I know you are committed, Commissioner, but I have to come after Commissioner Beaton on his information from the past. You’re a good boss. Thank you for coming to his defense. The previous administration which was no friend of this policy could only manage to inflate the cost to $17,000 per intersection. This is baffling considering if we apply this number to all

40,000 intersections of the city, the total cost is around 22 percent of that $3 billion number you and the administration touted– that the previous administration has touted. Are you aware of that, Mr. Beaton?
Yeah. I think we discussed it a little bit here, and as the Commissioner said, we’re happy to get into more detail about what it costs and what it takes to do this work.
Are you aware that Hoboken was able to roll out daylight en masse by starting with low-cost interventions like paint and plastic delineators which can start for as low as $1,500 per intersection?
We regularly talk to all of our neighbors about what and how they do things, and what they cost in different locations.
Are you also aware that Hoboken studied levels of interventions, including $2,000 to add some bike rack intersections?
I cannot speak to familiarity with every piece of Hoboken.

This is information I’m confident in, and it still comes nowhere near the cost that this administration is estimating. Last year, at the daylighting hearing, Council Member Won mentioned that DOT reported to her office that it would cost $10,000 to daylight an intersection which agrees with the Council’s analysis and which she stated public for the record. Do you disagree with your own agency’s analysis?
I’m sorry. I wasn’t totally following. But we’ve said it’s $10,000, right? That sounds the same.
They–
[interposing] I think it’s difficult to get into some of these details without everything in front of us. We’re more than happy to talk to you and make sure we are all looking at the same cost.
Can you just clarify, the $10,000–

[interposing] Sorry. Sorry, I’m not done with the line of questioning, Council Member. Even if DOT just did unhardened universal daylighting at certain intersections, it

only cost the city of Portland $700-$800 to erect four signs per an intersection. I understand this administration agrees with prior administration’s extremely questionable claim that unhardened daylighting is more dangerous in certain situations. But then, can this administration commit $400 million to implement universal hardened daylighting in our city? Every New Yorker deserves to feel safe and be safe in the areas where we live and work and play. Our seniors and children deserve to cross our streets without fear, and every New Yorker deserves better from their government. I remain disappointed with the resistance to this measure, but I’m grateful that Commissioner Flynn has committed not only in public conversations but in private conversations that he’s really committed to addressing this. Commissioner, I really, really am grateful for your leadership on this. I’m going to let Council Member Won ask questions on this specific issue, and then I’ll transition to other topic areas. Council Member Won?

Thank you so much, Chair Abreu. Getting a little frustrated. Okay, so why don’t we just ask in simpler terms. So, why don’t you explain to us your calculations for how

much intersections cost. Per intersection what is the actual cost? Not four intersections or four street or four sidewalks– however way you want to put it, how much does each intersection cost to daylight?
So, again, we’re happy to go through this with you in much more detail.
Yes, let’s go through it in detail now?
I’m happy to go through it in much more detail when we have all the figures in front of us and can be all looking at the same sheet [sic].
So, you came to this hearing on the budget without the figures in front of you for a budget hearing.
It costs roughly $10,000 per location.

So, per location he’s saying that it’s not $10,000 per location, because he’s defining location in a different way than the way that we define location. What is the $10,000 for? Give us the breakdown.
So, it’s about $10,000 per location which would be about $10 million for a thousand intersections.

Yes, we understand that which is why we were outside with over 100 advocates who have been calling year after year because hundreds of people die due to lack of daylighting with cars turning at intersections which I know, Commissioner, you already know because we’ve discussed this. Many people have discussed this with you before you took your position, and we understand that it’s going to be $10 million for a thousand intersections. So, help us understand what you mean by location? Do you mean location means four corners? What are you– why are you debunking what $10 million costs us to daylight.

Maybe I can try to clarify, if I may. So, every intersection, typical intersection has four corners, right? There’s two sides to each of that corner as the streets come together. So, if you can visualize that, there are actually eight. As Commissioner Beaton said, there’s eight potential places that you can do daylighting. So, when we say we can daylight

one corner or one intersection for $10,000, that’s simply one part of the eight, and that may be inadequate, right, in order to truly address safety at that intersection depending on what our engineers feel would be beneficial there. That’s why the $10,000 is over-simplifying the conversation. And it would help– you know, and I know we’re trying to take care of some of this here, but if you have time at another time, we’d love to sit there just like with a plan of a few streets and go through that with you.

So, I have a few follow-up questions. For daylighting, can you help me understand, how do you qualify what you deem as daylightable? Help me understand that. What are you qualifications to determine– because we went from the Mayor Zohran Mamdani, when he was an Assemblymember, he stood with me when a six-year-old was mauled by a car in Astoria, [inaudible] daylighting rally, and he demanded that we daylight every single intersection, and he’s been on record multiple times calling for universal daylighting. And now he has taken office and we’re now hearing the opposite of that from you all. So we want to understand, what do you qualify as somewhere that should be daylit because you are

saying that you no longer believe in universal daylighting, despite all of the times that the Mayor has gone on record in support of universal?

Thank you, Council Member. I just want to be clear that we share the same goal of eliminating traffic fatalities and we absolutely see daylighting as a key piece of that. We are all for figuring out and eager to work with you and other partners to understand the most effective and fast way to expand the use of daylighting. I just want to be clear on the record about that.
Okay, so how do you evaluate what locations are appropriate–
[interposing] Please wrap up, Council Member.
for daylighting?

We’ve focused on where it can be most effective. So, generally that’s where a driver would be able to make a legal turn. That’s where the daylighting can be most helpful, right? We want pedestrians to be visible and to be seen, and so if you think about one-way streets, some

corners are more helpful than others for daylighting, and that’s what we would want to prioritize.

Thank you. Alright. We’re going to transition now to a few other topic areas. Bus Action Plan– the Executive Plan includes additional city funding of $16.9 million and 70 headcount positions in fiscal 2027 that grows to $35 million and 104 additional positions in fiscal 2030 for the Bus Action Plan. How many miles of bus lanes will be built with this funding and how many will be new bus lanes?

Thank you, Chair. Yeah. So we’re thrilled with the level of investment. It’s a historic level of investment. It’s going to let us bring this program to a historic level of output. While I don’t have specific miles for this year because the program is kind of a dynamic thing that we’re developing and implementing, we’re expecting a historic level of output this year, significantly more than prior years.
Okay. Are you able to– do you know how much more that would be or–
[interposing] Unfortunately, I don’t have exact numbers.
Okay.
But I think it will be significantly more.
Than last year?
It’s what we’re on track for.
Alright. Once you get that information, if you could share that with us, that would be greatly appreciated. On average how much will each bus lane cost to install? Please be specific.
Might need a moment for that one.
Take your time.

It does vary quite a bit. You know, the– just the– for example, the red paint is about $4 a square foot in round numbers. But different lengths of bus lanes, if there’s more intersections, then you don’t have the red paint through the intersection, the costs are not the same for every mile in the city. So, this is a tremendous investment that the city has gotten us. It’s why we are planning it out street by street rather than just saying here’s an average, we’re

going to use this money to do as many bus lanes as we possibly can.
Thank you. What is the scope of the new positions, and is DOT hiring for these new positions now?
Well, it’s FY27 funding. So, as soon as we get the money we’re going to move quickly to staff up as quickly as we can. Tell all your friends. We’re going to need a lot of good–
[interposing] I have some folks in the audience here who are willing to apply for work, not kidding. So, we’re definitely going to spread the word.
Thank you.
What is the scope for these new position?

So, one of the things that we really did very thoughtfully and the Mayor funded is that this isn’t just more planners, you know, [inaudible] people to think about where we should do bus lanes. It includes the engineers who design them and it includes work throughout our operations. It includes people for

new concrete elements and new people for signal timing changes and just all the things that go into making a bus lane successful. So, we were very pleased that it’s not just sort of starter money. It’s really the money to plan and deliver the entire program.
Does any part of this funding go towards public engagement? How much and what specific actions will be taken to engage the public?

Absolutely. Public engagement is a key part of expanding any project, including bus lanes. And you know, just an example of that as was mentioned before, we have our Street Ambassador on Street Units that go out and meet people at bus stops, go business to business down corridors, and as we’re doing more of these projects we want to make sure we’re not just spreading that group more thinly and doing less outreach. We’re staffing up that group, for example, to do the same amount or more outreach with each of the projects that we do.
As a percentage, how much of this funding is dedicated to the implementation of bus lanes?

Thank you for the question, Chair. So, as Deputy Commissioner Beaton said, the bus lane can be many different things. I’d say on average it’s probably about 50 to 70 percent of it will be for the actual bus lanes and there will be support for all this work and the new need as well.

When you get the percentage, I would be grateful if you could share that with us. How many new bus shelters would be installed this year, particularly in transit deserts and along high ridership routes?

So, we’re going to be installing an additional 100 shelters this year, and thanks to the investment in this Executive Budget, we’re able to install another 100 per year for the next two years as well.
Great. With this funding, will DOT be able to meet the 30 miles of bus lanes as mandated by Local Law 195?
As I mentioned, we’re working as hard as we can to deliver as many and as much output as we can with the new funding.

With respect to bus rapid transit– bus rapid transit is a high-capacity bus-based urban transit system designed to combine the speed and efficiency of rail transit with flexibility and lower cost of buses. What factors does DOT consider when deciding to implement BRT?

Thank you for the question, Chair. Yeah, we’re really excited and we know there’s things we can learn from other cities around the world and really taking our bus priority efforts to the next level. We’re really excited that Flatbush Avenue is in construction as we speak which is really going to be one of the first on-the-ground examples of this type of approach. That’s something, you know, in the BRT spirit. I’m trying to remember now, the question was around–
[interposing] What factors did your agency consider when deciding to implement?

That’s right. Thank you. Yeah, so certainly ridership, certainly bus

speeds, but we also want to be looking forward to and think about, you know, what’s the potential folks may have seen in the housing announcement– I guess it was yesterday or the day before that the administration’s looking to sort of pair transit oriented development and affordable housing with things like BRT or other rapid transits. So, these are all factors that we consider, and we also work closely with our partners at the MTA because they’re also a big piece of this. A lot of the focus is on the street design and all that, but the other really important part is how MTA runs the buses and making sure we can maximize the speeds and the throughput.
Does DOT have a process in place at the moment for BRT approval?

So, we have a Transit Development Unit that works, as the Commissioner said, in very close partnership with the MTA and as part of looking at a corridor, one of the things that they do is look at all the data, look at the street design and figure out where these higher levels of investments are appropriate. So that's something that we’ve been starting to look at as part

of the new bus plan, and I think there’ll be more details as part of that.

Thank you. And I’ll just state for the record that, you know, my office has sent DOT a letter as well as advocates. I have sent DOT a letter in support of a BRT, bus rapid transit system, along 125th Street which would, you know, touch my district as well as other districts throughout Harlem. It’s something that I support, but now the ball is on the court is where I’ll leave it, but this is something that for us is very important we want to put on the record. I think it’s a great place for thinking big and really making sure that Harlem gets the attention it deserves. I’ll move over to cycling and micromobility. The Executive Plan adds funding for cycling and micromobility and includes $11.2 million and 45 new positions in fiscal 2027, $8.6 million and 52 new positions in 2028, reaching $22.8 million and 54 new positions by fiscal 2030. What will this funding go towards and how many bike lanes will be installed because of this funding?

Sure. So, in terms of what it goes towards, it’s a little bit

similar to what we talked about with the bus plan earlier where it’s both the planners and outreach specialists who can get the project moving, but it also really reinforces the operations around the agency in terms of our ability to deliver. So, it includes money for concrete work. It includes money for our marketing program. Again, we want to be very committed to not just saying we’re coming up with a lot of ideas, but to really delivering them.
On average, how much does it cost to install a bike lane? Do you have that information?

There’s definitely a lot of variables. I think as much or maybe in some ways even more than the bus lanes, because it depends on the specifics of the design of the bike lane, the concrete, you know, islands or traffic signal changes. So, I’m not sure if we have a rough range, or?

We can get back to you with the range, but as the Commissioner said, it’s a very wide range, right? A fully built-out greenway, you know– we did get a lot of

capital money in this budget as well, but the cost of that is very different from a painted on street lane.
